summary: This document proposes an additional endpoint for OAuth 2.0 authorization servers. Clients use it to tell the server that a refresh or access token is no longer needed, so the server can clean up credentials. A revocation request invalidates the token and, if applicable, other tokens from the same grant.

eli5.summary: When you finish using a key card, you hand it back and the building turns it off so nobody else can use it.

questions: how to revoke an oauth access token
how to revoke an oauth token
what is the oauth revocation endpoint
what does the revocation endpoint return
subtitle: A standard way for an OAuth client to tell the server that a token is no longer needed.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 let clients obtain access and refresh tokens but gave them no standard way to hand them back, so abandoned tokens and grants could linger after a logout or an uninstall.
tldr.mechanism: The authorization server offers a revocation endpoint. The client sends an HTTPS POST with the token (and optionally a type hint), and the server invalidates it and, depending on policy, related tokens from the same grant.
tldr.outcome: Servers can clean up credentials and session data, and users no longer see stale grants. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7009 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this RFC, so it remains the definition of OAuth 2.0 token revocation.

sections.title: Why Tokens Need Revoking
sections.content:
The OAuth 2.0 core specification, RFC 6749, defines several ways for a client to obtain access tokens and refresh tokens. RFC 7009 adds a mechanism to revoke both kinds. A token is a string representing an authorization grant that the resource owner issued to the client.

OAuth is often used to log in to a site or app. If the user logs out, changes identity or uninstalls the application, the client can now tell the authorization server. The server can then clean up data tied to the token, such as session data, and the underlying grant.

This prevents a valid grant from sitting around that the user does not know about, reduces abuse of abandoned tokens, and keeps invalidated grants out of any list of grants the server shows to the user.
sections.eli5: If you stop using an app, it should tell the website, so your old pass is torn up instead of left lying around.

sections.title: The Revocation Request
sections.content:
The client makes an HTTP POST to the token revocation endpoint. The URL must follow the rules in RFC 6749 Section 3.1, and clients MUST verify that it is an HTTPS URL, since the request carries plaintext credentials. How the client finds the endpoint is out of scope (server documentation or discovery may be used), but it must come from a trustworthy source.

The body uses application/x-www-form-urlencoded with two parameters: token (REQUIRED) is the token to revoke, and token_type_hint (OPTIONAL) is a hint such as access_token or refresh_token. If the server cannot find the token using the hint, it MUST search across all token types it supports, and it MAY ignore the hint. The client also authenticates as described in Section 2.3 of RFC 6749.

The server validates the client credentials (for a confidential client), checks that the token was issued to the requesting client, and then invalidates the token. Invalidation takes place immediately, though in practice there could be a propagation delay between servers. Clients must not use the token after receiving an HTTP 200 response.

Revoking one token may revoke others. Implementations MUST support revoking refresh tokens and SHOULD support revoking access tokens. If a refresh token is revoked and the server supports access token revocation, it SHOULD also invalidate all access tokens based on the same grant. If an access token is revoked, the server MAY revoke the refresh token as well.
sections.eli5: The app sends a note saying 'please cancel this pass', along with proof of who it is. The website checks the note and cancels the pass, and sometimes cancels the matching spare passes too.

sections.title: Responses and Errors
sections.content:
The server answers with HTTP status 200 if the token was revoked or if the client submitted an invalid token. An invalid token gets no error because the client could not do anything sensible with one, and the goal, an unusable token, is already achieved. The response body is ignored, and an invalid token type hint is ignored too.

Errors follow Section 5.2 of RFC 6749, plus one new code: unsupported_token_type, returned when the server does not support revoking the presented type of token (for example, an access token on a server that does not support that).

If the server responds with HTTP 503, the client must assume the token still exists and may retry after a reasonable delay. The server may send a Retry-After header to say how long the service is expected to be unavailable.
sections.eli5: If you hand back a pass that was already cancelled, the desk just says 'done'. If the desk is closed, come back a bit later.

sections.title: Browser Apps and Cross-Origin Use
sections.content:
If the endpoint is meant for use with user-agent-based applications, it MAY support Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS). For older browsers, it MAY also offer JSONP by accepting GET requests with an extra optional callback parameter naming a JavaScript function.

With JSONP, a success returns a call such as package.myCallback(); and an error returns the call with the error object, for example unsupported_token_type. The RFC warns that clients relying on JSONP should be aware that a malicious revocation endpoint may try to inject malicious code into the client.
sections.eli5: Web pages are picky about who they will talk to. These options let a web page still send its cancel note safely, though the older trick needs extra care.

sections.title: Access Token Styles and Revocation Cost
sections.content:
The Implementation Note explains that revoking access tokens depends on how a deployment issues them. Tokens may be self-contained, so a resource server can decide without asking the authorization server. Or they may be handles that refer to data stored at the authorization server, which the resource server must look up every time.

With handles, the authorization server can reject a revoked token when the resource server relays it. With self-contained tokens, some currently non-standardized backend interaction between the two servers may be needed if immediate revocation is wanted. Another option is short-lived access tokens that are refreshed with refresh tokens, which limits how long a revoked token stays usable.

The choice depends on the overall system design and the provider's risk analysis. The cost in state and communication is a result of the security properties wanted.
sections.eli5: Some passes can be checked by the guard alone, others need a phone call to the office. Cancelling is easier when the guard has to call, and harder when the pass checks itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the server does not support access token revocation, access tokens are not immediately invalidated when the matching refresh token is revoked, and deployments must account for that in their risk analysis. Revocation is cleanup: the RFC says it does not intend to provide countermeasures against token theft and abuse, and points to RFC 6749 and RFC 6819 for that.

Malicious clients could use the endpoint for denial-of-service attacks, and the same countermeasures as for the token endpoint MUST be applied. Invalid token type hints can cause extra database lookups, so care MUST be taken to prevent abuse.

Guessing tokens through this endpoint is not very useful to an attacker: the request needs a valid client_id or client credentials, and the token must belong to the requesting client. An attacker able to do that could do worse damage by using the token. Revoking it only makes the legitimate client prompt the user again.

Because the endpoint handles credentials, a counterfeit endpoint could capture valid tokens. Clients MUST authenticate the revocation endpoint, for example by certificate validation.
sections.eli5: Cancelling a pass cannot be used to steal it. The main danger is a fake desk, so the app must check it is talking to the real one.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the unsupported_token_type error in the OAuth Extensions Error Registry from RFC 6749. It also creates the OAuth Token Type Hints registry for values of token_type_hint.

New values are registered with Specification Required after a two-week review period on a mailing list, on the advice of one or more Designated Experts. The initial contents are access_token and refresh_token, both with the IETF as change controller.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed hint words, and the two starting words are already on it.
